unit-bio-u4.title: Biology 8 · Unit 4-1: The Cell Cycle and Mitosis
unit-bio-u4.srcName: G8_Cell Cycle and Mitosis_VA.pdf and the Mitosis Videos worksheet (Biology 8 · Unit 4, Drive)

summary.text: Her teacher's Unit 4 deck on the cell cycle and mitosis, plus the graded Mitosis Videos worksheet: why cells divide at all, the five kinds of asexual reproduction, chromatin and histones, the chromosome-versus-chromatid distinction and how to count both, diploid body cells against haploid gametes, the whole cycle through G1, S, G2 and G0, the three checkpoints, mitosis stage by stage through PMAT, and cytokinesis in an animal cell against a plant one.

why.text: Everything in genetics sits on this. Meiosis is the next unit and is taught almost entirely by contrast with mitosis, so a shaky grip here costs twice — and the chromosome-versus-chromatid counting turns up again in every inheritance problem she will meet this year.

objectives.text: Say what happens in each of G1, S, G2 and the mitotic phase, and why G0 is not one of them.
Count chromosomes and chromatids in a described set of structures, and explain why an X shape is one chromosome.
Put the stages of mitosis in order and name what happens to the chromosomes in each.
Tell diploid from haploid, and say why mitosis cannot produce a gamete.
Say how many checkpoints the cycle has, what each one checks, and what happens to a cell that fails one.
Explain why an animal cell pinches and a plant cell builds, and predict what a failure of cytokinesis alone would produce.

parentNote.text:
Built from two sources in her new Unit 4 folder: the teacher's own lecture deck (G8_Cell Cycle and Mitosis_VA.pdf, 39 slides) and the graded Mitosis Videos worksheet.

TWO THINGS ARE WORTH YOUR EYE, and both came out of reading the two sources against each other rather than either one alone.

FIRST — the graded worksheet asks about something the slides never cover. Question 5 of Video 1 asks how many checkpoints the cell cycle has, and question 6 asks what happens to a cell that cannot repair itself enough to pass one. The word 'checkpoint' appears twice on that worksheet and zero times across all 39 slides, and 'apoptosis' appears in neither — it is said aloud in the video. So the answers are only available to her if she actually watched the videos. Two cards here cover both (three checkpoints; apoptosis), and they are tagged as our addition rather than from her class material, because the deck cannot source them.

SECOND — one slide looks like a slip, and it contradicts her own homework. The cytokinesis slide reads 'Cell completely divides in two (chromosome reduction)'. Mitosis is not reductional; that is meiosis, which her class does next unit. The same slide says three lines above that each new nucleus has an identical set of chromosomes, and the worksheet's own fruit-fly question grades the opposite of the parenthetical — 8 chromosomes in, 8 in each daughter cell. This unit teaches the correct version (daughter cells keep the parent's chromosome number) and one question targets exactly that, since teaching her the slide's wording would cost her the mark on her own homework. Worth a quick check with her teacher if it comes up, in case it means something more specific in class.

No diagrams in this one, deliberately. The deck's phase photographs are textbook figures — one page is stamped Pearson copyright outright — so they are not ours to republish, the same call the Cells unit made. Public-domain mitosis diagrams do exist and could be added later, but every filename has to be verified before it ships rather than guessed. In the meantime one card describes what each phase actually looks like in a stained root tip, which is the skill the slides' photographs were there to teach.

nextUp.text: Start with the cards — the chromosome-versus-chromatid one and the counting one are the two her class drills hardest, and the rest of the unit leans on them.

cards.def:
**One parent cell splits its material between two new daughter cells.**
• 1 parent → 2 daughters
• For a single-celled organism, dividing IS reproduction — one cell becomes two organisms
• For a multicellular organism it is growth, repair, and making gametes
cards.hint: One becomes two. What that MEANS depends on whether the cell is the whole organism.

cards.def:
**By making MORE cells, not bigger ones.**
• A cell is capped in size by its surface area-to-volume ratio — the same limit from Unit 3
• Growing by inflating existing cells would strand the inside too far from the membrane
• So growth, tissue repair and regeneration all run on division
cards.hint: The surface-area limit never went away. Division is how a body works around it.

cards.def:
**One parent, and the offspring is genetically identical to it.**
• The parent passes ALL of its genes on — there is no second set to mix with
• In a multicellular organism it can mean growing an identical offspring from part of itself
cards.hint: One parent, all the genes, a copy rather than a blend.

cards.term: Five ways living things do it
cards.def:
**Binary fission, multiple fission, budding, fragmentation and clonal colonies.**
• Binary fission — a prokaryote divides once, 1 organism becomes 2
• Multiple fission — some protists divide several times at once, many offspring from one parent
• Budding — a hydra or jellyfish grows a smaller identical copy that detaches
• Fragmentation — a lost piece of a planarian or jumping cholla regrows a whole body
• Clonal colonies — aspen and fungi spread as genetically identical stands
cards.hint: Split once, split many, bud off, regrow from a piece, or spread as a clone.

cards.def:
**All the genetic information an organism needs, packaged as DNA.**
• Every cell of an organism carries the SAME genome — a skin cell and a liver cell hold identical DNA
• Prokaryote: one circular chromosome
• Eukaryote: multiple linear chromosomes
cards.hint: Same library in every cell. What differs is which books get read.

cards.def:
**DNA wound together with proteins called histones — the loose, uncoiled form DNA takes when the cell is not dividing.**
• The histones stop the chromosomes tangling and pack a great deal of DNA into a small space
• DNA plus histones forms a beadlike unit called a nucleosome
• Prokaryotic chromosomes have no histones
cards.hint: Thread loosely wound on spools. The spools are the histones.

cards.def:
**A chromatid is ONE strand; a chromosome is the whole structure, whether that is one strand or two joined ones.**
• After DNA is copied, a chromosome is two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere, in an X
• Before it is copied, the same chromosome is a single strand
• Think of the chromosome as one LETTER — an X is still one letter, even though you draw two lines
cards.hint: Count letters, not strokes.

cards.def:
**Count centromeres for chromosomes; count strands for chromatids.**
• One single strand = 1 chromosome, 1 chromatid
• One X shape = 1 chromosome, 2 chromatids
• The X never counts as two chromosomes while the centromere still holds it together
cards.hint: The join is what makes it one. Break the join and you have two.

cards.def:
**Body cells — everything that is not a sperm or an egg — and they carry two complete sets of each chromosome.**
• Two sets is what diploid means
• A human somatic cell has 46 chromosomes
• Most of your cells are somatic
cards.hint: Di- for two sets. Body cells keep both.

cards.def:
**Sperm and egg cells, carrying only ONE complete set of each chromosome.**
• One set is what haploid means
• A human gamete has 23 chromosomes
• Mitosis cannot make these — that is meiosis, and it is the next unit
cards.hint: Half the sets, so two can combine without doubling the count every generation.

cards.def:
**The whole series of events a cell goes through as it grows and divides — division is only one part of it.**
• The cell grows, receives a signal to divide, prepares (including copying all its DNA), then divides
• Two big stages: interphase, then the mitotic phase
cards.hint: Not just the splitting. The splitting is the short bit at the end.

cards.def:
**Growing and preparing: G1, then S, then G2. The cell spends at least 90% of its life here.**
• G1 — the cytoplasm doubles
• S — the DNA doubles
• G2 — double check
• Throughout all three the nucleus is intact, the nucleolus is visible, and the chromatin stays loose
cards.hint: Her teacher's own phrase: double the cytoplasm, double the DNA, double check.

cards.def:
**The first growth phase — the cell gets bigger and builds the proteins and organelles a new cell needs.**
• It is also doing its ordinary job the whole time
• The most VARIABLE phase in length between cell types — skin cells divide often, so their G1 is short
• At the end of G1 the cell either carries on into S or steps out into G0
cards.hint: Grow, build, and then the decision point.

cards.def:
**Synthesis — the DNA is replicated, and every chromosome ends up as two sister chromatids joined at the centromere.**
• The chromosomes stay in the loose chromatin state while this happens
• Once a cell enters S it almost always finishes the rest of the cycle
• A useful hook: S for Sister chromatids
cards.hint: This is the ONLY phase where the DNA is copied. Not mitosis.

cards.def:
**The second growth phase — the cell makes what mitosis will need and checks the copied DNA for errors.**
• Begins once all the DNA has been replicated
• Produces the proteins that drive mitosis to completion
• When G2 finishes, the cell leaves interphase and enters the M phase
cards.hint: Double check. Proofreading before the copy gets handed out.

cards.term: G0 — not in the cycle at all
cards.def:
**A resting state a cell drops into when it is not going to divide. It is NOT one of the cell cycle's phases.**
• Most of your cells are in G0 right now, doing their job rather than reproducing
• Mature neurons and muscle cells are in G0 permanently — which is why damage to those organs lasts
• Liver cells sit in G0 but can be pulled back in when the organ is damaged
• Skin cells are never in G0; they divide constantly
cards.hint: Opting out. Some cells opt out for good, some can be called back.

cards.def:
**Three points where the cell stops and checks itself before it is allowed to carry on: near the end of G1, near the end of G2, and partway through mitosis.**
• They check that the cell is big enough, that the DNA is undamaged, and that it was copied correctly
• Pass, and the cycle continues; fail, and the cell tries to repair the problem first
cards.hint: Three gates. Grow enough, copy it right, line it up right.

cards.def:
**Programmed cell death — what happens to a cell that cannot repair itself enough to pass a checkpoint.**
• It is the safe outcome, not a failure: a damaged cell dismantles itself on purpose
• A cell that ignores its checkpoints AND avoids apoptosis is how uncontrolled growth starts
cards.hint: The cell chooses to shut down rather than pass on a broken copy.

cards.def:
**Division of the NUCLEUS, in four stages: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase.**
• It produces two identical daughter nuclei
• Mitosis alone does not make two cells — that takes cytokinesis as well
cards.hint: Pro, Meta, Ana, Telo. The nucleus divides; the cell has not yet.

cards.def:
**The chromosomes bundle up tight, the spindle forms, and the nuclear envelope starts to break down.**
• Condensing is what makes the chromosomes visible under a microscope for the first time
• The spindle is part of the cytoskeleton; in animal cells the centrioles move apart as it forms
• Think of loose string being rolled into a ball
cards.hint: Bundle up, build the machinery, open the nucleus.

cards.def:
**The spindle lines every chromosome up across the middle of the cell, on the metaphase plate.**
• Middle — Metaphase. The M's line up too
• Nothing separates yet; this is the arranging step
cards.hint: A single row across the equator of the cell.

cards.def:
**The sister chromatids are pulled apart and dragged to opposite ends of the cell.**
• Away — Anaphase
• The moment they separate, each former chromatid counts as a chromosome of its own
• The spindle does the pulling
cards.hint: The X splits into two, and the two halves travel in opposite directions.

cards.def:
**The chromosomes unbundle, the spindle breaks down, and two new nuclear envelopes form.**
• Two — Telophase: two nuclei now exist
• Cytokinesis usually happens at the same time
cards.hint: Undo prophase, twice over.

cards.def:
**Division of the CYTOPLASM — this is the step that actually produces two separate cells.**
• Animal cells pinch inward with a cleavage furrow, a contracting ring of microfilaments
• Plant cells build a cell plate across the middle, which becomes a new cell wall
• A plant cell cannot pinch — its cell wall is rigid, so it has to build a divider instead
cards.hint: Mitosis divides the nucleus. This divides everything else.

cards.def:
**In an onion root tip the whole cycle takes about 24 hours, and roughly 23 of them are interphase.**
• G1 about 5-6 hours, S about 10-12, G2 about 4-6, and M about 1
• Even in a cell that divides as fast as it can, dividing is the short part
cards.hint: A whole day of preparing for one hour of dividing.

cards.term: Spotting the phases down a microscope
cards.def:
**In a stained root tip you tell the phase from what the dark material inside the cell is doing.**
• Interphase — one round, evenly dark nucleus, no separate threads
• Prophase — threads visible inside a nucleus that is losing its outline
• Metaphase — a tight dark line straight across the middle
• Anaphase — two clumps pulling apart, often V-shaped
• Telophase — two separate round clumps, a wall or furrow appearing between them
cards.hint: Look for where the dark stuff is: one blob, a line, two clumps moving, two blobs.

cards.def:
**Identical copies — for reproduction in single-celled eukaryotes, and for growth and repair in multicellular ones.**
• The two new cells are exact duplicates, so they can do the same job the parent did
• Errors in division cause abnormal chromosome numbers, genetic disorders, and uncontrolled growth such as cancer
cards.hint: Copies, so the replacement can do the original's job.

questions.q: A cell is described as having a nucleus with a visible nucleolus, loose chromatin, and no spindle. Which part of the cell cycle is it in?
opts: Interphase
Prophase
Anaphase
Telophase
questions.hint: Loose chromatin and an intact nucleus mean nothing has started condensing yet.
steps: The nucleus is intact and the nucleolus is visible, so the nuclear envelope has not broken down.
The chromatin is loose, so the chromosomes have not condensed.
No spindle has formed, so prophase has not begun.
All three are the signature of interphase.

ex.main: **Interphase.** An intact nucleus, a visible nucleolus and loose chromatin together mean the cell is growing and working, not dividing — that is interphase, where cells spend at least 90% of their lives.
ex.tip: Condensed chromosomes are the first visible sign that mitosis has started.

questions.q: In which single phase of the cell cycle is DNA replicated?
opts: G1 phase
S phase
G2 phase
Prophase
questions.hint: Its name is the clue, and so is the thing it produces.
steps: G1 is growth — the cytoplasm doubles, not the DNA.
S stands for synthesis, and it is where sister chromatids are produced.
G2 comes after replication and checks the copy.
So replication happens in S.

ex.main: **S phase.** Synthesis is where the DNA is copied and each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids. A common slip is to think the copying happens during mitosis — by the time mitosis starts, the copy has already been made and checked.
ex.tip: S for Synthesis, and S for Sister chromatids.

questions.q: A structure is described as five separate pieces: four of them are X-shaped, and one is a single strand. How many chromosomes and how many chromatids are there?
opts: 5 chromosomes, 5 chromatids
9 chromosomes, 9 chromatids
5 chromosomes, 9 chromatids
4 chromosomes, 8 chromatids
questions.hint: Count the separate pieces for one number and the strands for the other.
steps: Each separate piece is one chromosome, whatever its shape — so five pieces means five chromosomes.
An X shape is two chromatids joined at a centromere: four X shapes give eight chromatids.
The single strand adds one more chromatid, making nine.
So 5 chromosomes and 9 chromatids.

ex.main: **5 chromosomes, 9 chromatids.** A chromosome is the whole structure — think of it as one letter, and an X is one letter even though you draw two strokes. A chromatid is one strand, so every X contributes two and every single strand contributes one.
ex.tip: Count centromeres for chromosomes, strands for chromatids.

questions.q: Which phase is described by: the chromosomes condense, the spindle forms, and the nuclear envelope begins to break down?
opts: Cytokinesis
Metaphase
Anaphase
Prophase
questions.hint: This is the setting-up stage — nothing has moved to the middle or the ends yet.
steps: Condensing chromosomes is the first visible event of mitosis.
The spindle has to exist before it can line anything up or pull anything apart.
The nuclear envelope must open before the spindle can reach the chromosomes.
All three happen in prophase.

ex.main: **Prophase.** It is the preparation stage: bundle the chromosomes up so they can be moved without tearing, build the spindle that will move them, and open the nucleus so it can reach them.
ex.tip: Nothing is lined up and nothing is separating yet — that is what makes it prophase.

questions.q: What does a cell in G0 do?
opts: Its ordinary job, without preparing to divide
Copies its DNA more slowly than usual
Repairs damaged DNA before re-entering mitosis
Condenses its chromosomes and waits for a signal
questions.hint: The name means it has stepped out of the numbered phases entirely.
steps: G0 is not one of the cell cycle's phases — it is outside the cycle.
A cell there is not preparing to divide at all.
It carries on doing whatever that cell type does.
So it does its ordinary job without preparing to divide.

ex.main: **Its ordinary job, without preparing to divide.** Most of your cells are in G0 right now. Mature neurons and muscle cells are there permanently, which is a large part of why damage to those organs is lasting; liver cells can be pulled back into the cycle when the organ is injured.
ex.tip: G0 is not a phase of the cycle. It is being out of the cycle.

questions.q: In an animal cell, what physically separates the two daughter cells at the end of division?
opts: A cell plate built across the middle
A cleavage furrow pinching inward
The spindle pushing the two halves apart
The nuclear envelope splitting in two
questions.hint: Think about whether an animal cell has anything rigid to build against.
steps: An animal cell has no cell wall, so it can deform.
A contracting ring of microfilaments squeezes the membrane inward.
That inward pinch is the cleavage furrow.
A cell plate is what a plant cell builds instead, because a rigid wall cannot pinch.

ex.main: **A cleavage furrow pinching inward.** The membrane is pulled in by a contracting ring of microfilaments until the cell is squeezed in two. A plant cell cannot do this — its wall is rigid — so it builds a cell plate across the middle instead, which becomes a new cell wall.
ex.tip: Pinch if you are soft, build a wall if you are not.

questions.q: How many checkpoints does the cell cycle use to make sure the cell and its DNA are ready to divide?
opts: Two
One
Three
Five
questions.hint: There is one near the end of each of two interphase stages, and one during the division itself.
steps: One sits near the end of G1, checking the cell is big enough and its DNA is undamaged.
One sits near the end of G2, checking the DNA was copied correctly.
One sits partway through mitosis, checking the chromosomes are lined up properly.
That is three.

ex.main: **Three.** Each one stops the cycle until a particular thing checks out — big enough, copied correctly, lined up correctly. A cell that cannot repair a problem enough to pass undergoes apoptosis, which is the safe outcome rather than a failure.
ex.tip: Grow enough, copy it right, line it up right.

questions.q: A cat's body cell contains 38 chromosomes. After that cell divides by mitosis, how many chromosomes are in EACH daughter cell?
opts: It depends on which daughter cell
questions.hint: Mitosis makes identical copies. What would 'identical' have to mean about the count?
steps: The DNA was replicated in S phase, so the cell entered mitosis with 38 chromosomes of two chromatids each.
In anaphase the sister chromatids separate, and each half goes to one end.
Each end therefore receives one full set of 38.
So each daughter cell has 38.

ex.main: **38.** Mitosis produces two cells genetically identical to the parent, and identical includes the chromosome count. Halving the number is meiosis, which makes gametes and is the next unit — that is the single commonest mix-up between the two.
ex.tip: Replication happened first. That is what lets both daughters get a full set.

questions.q: Why does a growing animal make more cells rather than simply growing the cells it already has?
opts: Volume grows faster than surface area, so a large cell cannot supply its own interior
Each cell holds only a fixed amount of DNA, which caps how large it can grow
Cells wear out after a set number of days and have to be replaced on a schedule
A cell that grows past a certain size is pushed out of the cell cycle into G0
questions.hint: The limit is about what has to cross the membrane, not about the membrane's strength.
steps: Everything a cell needs enters and leaves across its surface.
As a cell gets bigger, its volume grows faster than its surface area.
So a large cell has relatively less membrane serving relatively more interior.
Dividing keeps each cell small enough for its own surface to supply it.

ex.main: **Volume grows faster than surface area, so a large cell cannot supply its own interior.** This is the same surface area-to-volume limit from the cells unit, and it is why growth has to mean more cells rather than bigger ones. Animal cells have no cell wall at all, so that is not the constraint.
ex.tip: The membrane is the loading dock. Doubling the warehouse does not double the dock.

questions.q: During which stage do the sister chromatids first become separate chromosomes?
opts: Prophase
Anaphase
Metaphase
Telophase
questions.hint: The moment the centromere lets go is the moment the counting changes.
steps: In prophase and metaphase the sister chromatids are still joined at the centromere.
While they are joined, the pair counts as one chromosome.
In anaphase the spindle pulls them apart.
The instant they separate, each one counts as a chromosome in its own right.

ex.main: **Anaphase.** A chromosome is defined by its centromere, so while two chromatids are joined they are one chromosome. Separating them momentarily doubles the cell's chromosome count — and then the cell divides, which brings each daughter back to the normal number.
ex.tip: Away — Anaphase. The count changes at the moment of separation.

questions.q: A cell is found with a tight dark line of chromosomes running straight across its middle, and no nuclear envelope. Which stage is it in?
opts: Anaphase
Interphase
Metaphase
Prophase
questions.hint: One row, across the centre, and nothing moving apart yet.
steps: The missing nuclear envelope rules out interphase — it broke down in prophase.
The chromosomes are in a single line rather than scattered, so prophase is finished.
Nothing has moved to the ends, so anaphase has not started.
A single row across the middle is the metaphase plate.

ex.main: **Metaphase.** The spindle has lined every chromosome up on the metaphase plate across the centre of the cell. It is the arranging step — nothing separates until anaphase.
ex.tip: Middle — Metaphase. Both start with M.

questions.q: Which pair of cells CANNOT be produced by mitosis?
opts: Root tip cells and leaf cells
Skin cells and liver cells
Muscle cells and nerve cells
Sperm and egg cells
questions.hint: Think about how many complete sets of chromosomes each kind of cell carries.
steps: Mitosis produces cells genetically identical to the parent, with the same chromosome count.
Body cells are diploid — two complete sets — and mitosis keeps them that way.
Sperm and egg cells are haploid: one complete set, half the number.
Producing them means halving the count, which mitosis cannot do.

ex.main: **Sperm and egg cells.** Gametes are haploid, and mitosis always produces cells with the same chromosome number as the parent. Making them requires meiosis, which is the next unit.
ex.tip: Mitosis copies. Only meiosis halves.

questions.q: In a root tip where the whole cell cycle takes 24 hours, roughly 23 of those hours are spent in interphase. What does that predict about a photograph of many cells from that root tip?
opts: The large majority of cells will be in interphase
Cells will be spread evenly across all the phases
Most cells will be caught in metaphase, the longest mitotic stage
About half the cells will be dividing at any moment
questions.hint: In a random snapshot, how likely a cell is to be caught in a stage depends on how long it lasts.
steps: A snapshot catches each cell wherever it happens to be.
The longer a stage lasts, the more cells will be in it at any one moment.
Interphase takes about 23 of the 24 hours.
So the large majority of cells in the picture will be in interphase.

ex.main: **The large majority of cells will be in interphase.** This is exactly why counting cells in each stage on a slide tells you how long each stage takes — the proportion you see IS the proportion of time spent there. Even in a cell dividing as fast as it can, dividing is the short part.
ex.tip: A snapshot is a sample of time, not a sample of stages.

questions.q: A cell reaches the end of G2 with DNA damage it has not been able to repair. What is the normal outcome?
opts: It divides anyway and the damage is repaired afterwards
It undergoes apoptosis rather than dividing
It returns to G1 and repeats the whole cycle
It enters G0 permanently and keeps working
questions.hint: The point of a checkpoint is to stop something from being passed on.
steps: The G2 checkpoint exists to catch exactly this — DNA that was not copied correctly.
A cell that can repair the damage does so, then carries on.
A cell that cannot repair it must not hand a broken copy to two daughter cells.
So it undergoes apoptosis, programmed cell death.

ex.main: **It undergoes apoptosis rather than dividing.** Apoptosis is the safe outcome, not a malfunction — the cell dismantles itself on purpose so the damage goes no further. A cell that ignores its checkpoints AND escapes apoptosis is how uncontrolled growth begins.
ex.tip: Better one cell lost than two cells wrong.

questions.q: Put these four events in order, from earliest to latest.
opts: The DNA is replicated
The chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell
The sister chromatids are pulled to opposite ends
A cleavage furrow pinches the cell in two
questions.hint: Copy it, arrange it, separate it, then split the cell itself.
steps: Replication comes first, in S phase, long before mitosis starts.
Lining up across the middle is metaphase.
Pulling the chromatids apart is anaphase, which follows metaphase.
The cleavage furrow is cytokinesis, which finishes the job.

ex.main: **Replicate, line up, separate, pinch.** The order matters because each step depends on the one before it: you cannot line up chromosomes you have not copied, cannot separate chromatids you have not lined up, and cannot usefully split a cell whose nucleus has not divided.
ex.tip: S phase happens hours before mitosis begins — it is easy to forget it is part of the same cycle.

questions.q: A drug blocks the spindle from forming, but leaves everything else working. Where does the cell get stuck, and why?
opts: At telophase, because the nuclear envelope cannot reform
At S phase, because the DNA cannot be copied without a spindle
At metaphase, because nothing can line the chromosomes up
At G1, because the cell cannot receive the signal to divide
questions.hint: Work out the first job in the sequence that the spindle is actually responsible for.
steps: The spindle is not involved in copying DNA, so S phase runs normally.
Prophase can begin — the chromosomes condense on their own.
But the spindle is what lines the chromosomes up on the metaphase plate.
With no spindle the cell cannot get past that arranging step, so it stalls at metaphase.

ex.main: **At metaphase, because nothing can line the chromosomes up.** The spindle both arranges the chromosomes and later pulls the chromatids apart, so removing it stops the process at the first of those jobs. This is not hypothetical — several real cancer drugs work exactly this way, and the mitotic checkpoint is what holds the cell there.
ex.tip: Trace the first step that actually needs the missing part.

questions.q: Two cells from the same organism are examined. One has 12 chromosomes, the other has 6. What is the most likely explanation?
opts: The two cells came from different tissues with different genomes
The second cell is partway through anaphase
The first cell failed a checkpoint and doubled its DNA
The first is a body cell and the second is a gamete
questions.hint: Halving is a specific, normal thing that happens to one kind of cell.
steps: Every cell of an organism carries the same genome, so different tissues is not the explanation.
A body cell is diploid — two complete sets.
A gamete is haploid — one complete set, so half the number.
Six is half of twelve, which fits a gamete against a body cell exactly.

ex.main: **The first is a body cell and the second is a gamete.** Diploid means two complete sets, haploid means one. Anaphase would momentarily raise the count rather than halve it, and every cell of one organism carries the same genome — what differs between tissues is which genes get used, not which genes are present.
ex.tip: Half the chromosomes is the signature of a gamete, and only meiosis makes them.

questions.q: Why does a plant cell build a cell plate instead of pinching inward the way an animal cell does?
opts: Its rigid cell wall cannot be pulled inward
Its chloroplasts would be damaged by pinching
Plant cells divide too slowly for a furrow to form
Its central vacuole holds the membrane in place
questions.hint: Ask what an animal cell has that lets it deform, and whether a plant cell has it.
steps: A cleavage furrow works by contracting a ring of microfilaments that pulls the membrane inward.
That requires a flexible outer boundary.
A plant cell is enclosed in a rigid cell wall, which will not deform that way.
So it builds a divider across the middle instead, which becomes a new cell wall.

ex.main: **Its rigid cell wall cannot be pulled inward.** The wall that gives a plant cell its shape is exactly what stops it dividing the way an animal cell does — so instead of squeezing from the outside in, it assembles a cell plate from the inside out.
ex.tip: Same goal, opposite direction, because of one structure the two cells do not share.

questions.q: A cell type is described as being in G0 permanently. What does that predict about the tissue it belongs to?
opts: That tissue will grow faster than tissues whose cells divide
Damage to that tissue will not be repaired by replacing the cells
That tissue is the most likely place for cancer to start
That tissue will replace its cells more often than most
questions.hint: If a cell never re-enters the cycle, what can the tissue no longer do?
steps: Replacing a lost cell requires a cell that divides.
A cell permanently in G0 has left the cycle and will not divide again.
So there is nothing to produce replacements.
Damage to that tissue therefore is not repaired by replacing the cells.

ex.main: **Damage to that tissue will not be repaired by replacing the cells.** Mature neurons and muscle cells are the standard examples, and it is a large part of why nerve and heart damage is lasting. It also makes cancer LESS likely there, not more — uncontrolled growth requires cells that divide.
ex.tip: No division means no replacement, and also no runaway division.

questions.q: Mitosis and cytokinesis are described as two separate processes. What would a cell look like if mitosis completed normally but cytokinesis failed?
opts: One cell with a single nucleus holding twice the DNA
Two cells, each with no nucleus
One cell containing two complete nuclei
Two cells joined by a permanent cleavage furrow
questions.hint: Name exactly what each of the two processes divides, then remove one of them.
steps: Mitosis divides the nucleus, producing two identical daughter nuclei.
Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm, producing two separate cells.
If mitosis finishes, two complete nuclei exist.
If cytokinesis fails, they are never separated — so both sit in one cell.

ex.main: **One cell containing two complete nuclei.** This is the cleanest way to see that the two processes are genuinely separate: mitosis is nuclear division and cytokinesis is cytoplasmic division. Multinucleate cells are real — human skeletal muscle fibres are a normal example.
ex.tip: Mitosis divides the nucleus. It does not, by itself, make two cells.
